sections.html:
Richmond is the seat of Madison County, in the Bluegrass region about 26 miles south of Lexington. The city has 40,663 people as of July 2025, up from 35,164 in 2020, spread over 15,202 households. Eastern Kentucky University anchors the local economy, the median age is 29.1 years, and 37.4 percent of households are one person. That mix keeps demand steady for rentals and starter homes.

Housing here leans toward renting. Fewer than four in ten households own their home, so a large share of the houses that change hands are rentals or former rentals.

These figures come from the five year survey ending 2024.

If you own a house with tenants in it, have the leases and rent records ready. Buyers will ask for them early.

sections.h2: Selling a rental or inherited house
sections.html: An owner who inherited a rental, or who is tired of managing one, has three paths: sell with tenants in place, wait for the lease to end, or close with a buyer who takes over the lease. Read the lease end date and the notice terms before you answer any offer. A cash buyer who accepts the property as is can skip the cleanout and repair cycle that usually follows a tenant move-out.

sections.h2: City permit and code rules that can slow a sale
sections.html:
Richmond's building inspection office (859-625-6428) enforces the 2018 Kentucky Building Code and related standards. If a prior owner finished a basement, added a deck or swapped a furnace without paperwork, the gap can surface during a buyer's inspection.

  • Permits are required for new construction, structural additions, basement remodels that change the occupant load, and room additions.
  • Sheds and garages need a permit once they reach 200 square feet in a residential setting.
  • Decks and porches need one at 200 square feet, at 30 inches above the ground, or when roofed or attached to the dwelling.
  • Furnace, air conditioner and electrical panel replacements need permits, and electrical and HVAC installers who are not the homeowner need a city business license.
  • Exterior work inside the H1 historic district goes before the Architectural Review Board, and ground mounted solar is not allowed in residential sections.
  • Permit work is inspected in stages, typically footer, foundation, slab, envelope, framing or rough-in, and a final. The permit holder must call for each one.

If a seller built a deck or finished a room years ago, ask the office whether a permit was ever pulled and request a final sign-off on any open one. Applications can be filed through the city's online Accela portal or on paper at the office. Plumbing permits come from the state plumbing division or the local plumbing inspector rather than the city.

Codes Enforcement applies the property maintenance code published by the International Code Council. The board meets on the second Wednesday of each month at 5:30 p.m. at City Hall, 239 W. Main Street. Call 859-625-6404 about an open case before you list, so you can describe its status plainly to a buyer instead of having it turn up in due diligence.

sections.h2: Location and age of the house
sections.html: Interstate 75 runs along the west side of the city with three exits, and U.S. 25 and 421 form the eastern bypass toward Lexington. Berea is about 14 miles south on U.S. 25. Madison County Schools serves the city. Summers run hot and damp, which puts the age of the air conditioner high on an inspector's list.

sections.h2: Property tax bill and who pays
sections.html:
Madison County's Sheriff collects the bill at 135 W Irvine, Suite B01, with mail and online portal options as well. The office is open weekdays from 8:00 to 4:30 and answers at 859-623-1511. Exemptions for homestead and disability go through the county PVA at 859-623-5410. Card and online payments are accepted. A mortgage servicer may pay from escrow, yet the owner still receives a bill notice and should confirm that payment went out.

KRS 134.015 treats the tax as the debt of whoever held title on the January 1 assessment date. Paying everything on or before November 1 saves 2 percent, the plain amount is due until December 31, and the late charge is 5 percent in January and 10 percent once February arrives. Buyers and sellers commonly prorate the year's tax at closing, with the current owner answerable for seeing that the bill gets paid.

sections.h2: Steps for a Richmond owner who wants out fast
sections.html:
Start with the paperwork you can pull in an afternoon. Call the building inspection office and ask whether any permit on the house is still open. Call Codes Enforcement and ask the same about maintenance cases. Check with the Sheriff that the current tax bill is paid, since the debt follows whoever held title on January 1.

Next, decide how the house will be sold. A listing brings showings, an inspection and repair requests, plus a commission at closing. A cash offer on the house as it stands skips most of that, and the closing date is often your choice. Weigh the final net, not the headline number, and ask each buyer in writing what they expect you to fix, if anything.

If tenants live there, tell them early and share what the lease says about notice. Plan on handing the buyer copies of the leases and the deposit records at closing.

KRS 133.045 opens the real property roll to public inspection for 13 days beginning in early May, with Saturday hours. A taxpayer who wants to appeal must first ask the PVA for a conference. The window comes around each spring.

A seller can use the conference to learn how the value was built. Bring recent neighborhood sales and ask the PVA to walk through the calculation. A value above what nearby houses fetch raises the bill that follows the house to its next owner.

The seller bears Kentucky's deed transfer tax, set at $0.50 per $500 of the price, counting any partial block (KRS 142.050). Other items on the statement include the prorated property tax, payoff of any mortgage or lien, and an agent's commission if you list. A cash sale drops the commission and repair work from that list, so compare the final net rather than the headline price.

Before closing day, collect the payoff letter from your lender, the latest tax bill, and any permit paperwork for work done on the house. Having those in hand keeps the closing date from slipping.

faqs.q: Is a permit needed to swap out a Richmond furnace?
faqs.a: Yes. Furnace and air conditioner change-outs are on the city's permit list, and the finished work gets inspected. Phone Building Inspections at 859-625-6428 before a contractor starts, because a missing permit tends to surface once a buyer orders an inspection.

faqs.q: Is Richmond mostly a renter city?
faqs.a: Yes. Only 38.3 percent of households own their home, so roughly 62 percent rent.

faqs.q: Where does a Richmond owner send the county tax payment?
faqs.a: To the Madison County Sheriff at 135 W Irvine, Suite B01, through the sheriff's online tax portal or by check. Never mail cash. Staff answer at 859-623-1511 on weekdays.

faqs.q: Can a Richmond house with code violations be sold?
faqs.a: Yes, though calling Codes Enforcement first at 859-625-6404 saves surprises. Its board meets on the second Wednesday of the month at 5:30 p.m., and knowing the status of an open case lets you describe it plainly to a buyer.

faqs.q: Which transfer tax applies to a Richmond sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays 50 cents on every $500 of price, counting partial blocks. Foreclosure deeds and some family transfers are exempt.
